name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q01 - Levels of organisation across animal phyla

questiontext.text:
Match the levels of organisation with the corresponding animal phyla and select the correct option.

List I (Level of Organisation)List II (Phylum)
A. Cellular levelI. Coelenterata
B. Tissue levelII. Annelida
C. Organ levelIII. Porifera
D. Organ-system levelIV. Platyhelminthes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although all members of Kingdom Animalia are multicellular, they exhibit progressively complex patterns of cellular organisation ranging from loose cell aggregates to functional organ systems.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
In sponges (Porifera), cells are arranged as loose cell aggregates, representing the cellular level of organisation. In coelenterates, cells performing the same function are arranged into tissues, exhibiting the tissue level of organisation. In Platyhelminthes, tissues are grouped together to form specialised organs, showing the organ level of organisation. In higher phyla such as Annelida, organs associate to form functional organ systems, representing the organ-system level of organisation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each level of organisation to its respective phylum gives Cellular level with Porifera, Tissue level with Coelenterata, Organ level with Platyhelminthes, and Organ-system level with Annelida (A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q02 - Common names and scientific names of Porifera and Cnidaria

questiontext.text:
Match the common names of animals with their scientific names and select the correct option.

List I (Common Name)List II (Scientific Name)
A. Portuguese man-of-warI. Pennatula
B. Bath spongeII. Physalia
C. Sea-penIII. Meandrina
D. Brain coralIV. Euspongia

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Members of Phylum Porifera and Phylum Coelenterata (Cnidaria) have distinct common names alongside their binomial or generic scientific names.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Physalia is commonly known as the Portuguese man-of-war. Euspongia is a member of Phylum Porifera commonly called the bath sponge. Pennatula is a cnidarian commonly known as the sea-pen, and Meandrina is a coral commonly called the brain coral.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each common name with its scientific name gives Portuguese man-of-war with Physalia, Bath sponge with Euspongia, Sea-pen with Pennatula, and Brain coral with Meandrina (A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q03 - Excretory and osmoregulatory structures across phyla

questiontext.text:
Match the excretory/osmoregulatory structures with their respective animal phyla and select the correct option.

List I (Excretory Structure)List II (Phylum)
A. Flame cellsI. Annelida
B. NephridiaII. Arthropoda
C. Malpighian tubulesIII. Hemichordata
D. Proboscis glandIV. Platyhelminthes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different non-chordate phyla have evolved specialised structures for osmoregulation and the removal of nitrogenous wastes.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
In Platyhelminthes (flatworms), specialised cells called flame cells help in osmoregulation and excretion. In Annelida, tubular structures called nephridia perform osmoregulation and excretion. In Arthropoda, excretion takes place through Malpighian tubules. In Hemichordata, the excretory organ is the proboscis gland.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each excretory structure with its phylum yields Flame cells with Platyhelminthes, Nephridia with Annelida, Malpighian tubules with Arthropoda, and Proboscis gland with Hemichordata (A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q04 - Distinctive anatomical structures and animal phyla

questiontext.text:
Match the distinctive anatomical structures with the phyla in which they are found and select the correct option.

List I (Structure)List II (Phylum)
A. ChoanocytesI. Coelenterata
B. CnidoblastsII. Mollusca
C. Comb platesIII. Porifera
D. RadulaIV. Ctenophora

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each major non-chordate phylum possesses diagnostic anatomical structures that aid in feeding, locomotion, or defense.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Choanocytes (collar cells) line the spongocoel and canals in Porifera. Cnidoblasts (stinging cells containing nematocysts) are used for anchorage, defense, and prey capture in Coelenterata (Cnidaria). Eight external rows of ciliated comb plates help in locomotion in Ctenophora. The radula is a file-like rasping organ for feeding present in the mouth of Mollusca.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each structure to its phylum gives Choanocytes with Porifera, Cnidoblasts with Coelenterata, Comb plates with Ctenophora, and Radula with Mollusca (A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q05 - Coelom and segmentation patterns with animal examples

questiontext.text:
Match the body cavity and segmentation characteristics with the appropriate animal examples and select the correct option.

List I (Body Plan Feature)List II (Example)
A. AcoelomateI. Pila
B. PseudocoelomateII. Taenia
C. Coelomate (unsegmented)III. Pheretima
D. Coelomate (metamerically segmented)IV. Ascaris

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bilateral triploblastic animals are classified by the presence and nature of the coelom as well as the presence or absence of metameric segmentation.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Taenia (tapeworm) belongs to Platyhelminthes, which are acoelomates lacking a body cavity. Ascaris (roundworm) belongs to Aschelminthes, which are pseudocoelomates. Pila (apple snail) belongs to Mollusca, which are coelomates with an unsegmented body. Pheretima (earthworm) belongs to Annelida, which are coelomates exhibiting metameric segmentation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each feature with its example gives Acoelomate with Taenia, Pseudocoelomate with Ascaris, unsegmented coelomate with Pila, and metamerically segmented coelomate with Pheretima (A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q06 - Ecological and economic roles of arthropods

questiontext.text:
Match the categories of arthropods with their correct examples and select the right option.

List I (Category)List II (Example)
A. Living fossilI. Locusta
B. Gregarious pestII. Laccifer
C. VectorIII. Limulus
D. Economically important insectIV. Anopheles

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phylum Arthropoda includes diverse species with distinct ecological and economic roles, such as pollinators, lac/silk producers, disease vectors, agricultural pests, and evolutionary relics.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Limulus (king crab) is an arthropod classified as a living fossil. Locusta (locust) is a well-known gregarious pest. Anopheles (along with Culex and Aedes) is a mosquito vector. Laccifer (lac insect) is an economically important insect alongside Apis and Bombyx.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each category to its example gives Living fossil with Limulus, Gregarious pest with Locusta, Vector with Anopheles, and Economically important insect with Laccifer (A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q07 - Specialised features of Cyclostomata, Chondrichthyes, and Osteichthyes

questiontext.text:
Match the aquatic vertebrates with their characteristic group or specialised feature and select the correct option.

List I (Feature / Group)List II (Animal)
A. Jawless ectoparasite (Cyclostomata)I. Trygon
B. Cartilaginous fish with electric organsII. Torpedo
C. Cartilaginous fish with poison stingIII. Hippocampus
D. Marine bony fish (Osteichthyes)IV. Petromyzon

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aquatic vertebrates include jawless cyclostomes (Agnatha), cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes), and bony fishes (Osteichthyes), each with distinct morphological and defensive adaptations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Petromyzon (lamprey) is a jawless vertebrate belonging to Class Cyclostomata that lives as an ectoparasite on some fishes. Among Chondrichthyes, Torpedo possesses electric organs, whereas Trygon (sting ray) possesses a poison sting. Hippocampus (sea horse) is a marine bony fish belonging to Class Osteichthyes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each feature to the corresponding animal gives Jawless ectoparasite with Petromyzon, Cartilaginous fish with electric organs with Torpedo, Cartilaginous fish with poison sting with Trygon, and Marine bony fish with Hippocampus (A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q08 - Diagnostic features of vertebrate classes

questiontext.text:
Match the diagnostic combinations of features with the corresponding vertebrate classes and select the correct option.

List I (Diagnostic Features)List II (Vertebrate Class)
A. Placoid scales and persistent notochordI. Amphibia
B. Operculum and air bladderII. Chondrichthyes
C. Moist scaleless skin and cloacaIII. Reptilia
D. Dry cornified skin and epidermal scutesIV. Osteichthyes

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vertebrate classes under Gnathostomata are distinguished by their endoskeleton, skin coverings, gill covers, buoyancy organs, and body openings.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Chondrichthyes have tough skin with minute placoid scales and a notochord that is persistent throughout life. Osteichthyes possess four pairs of gills covered by an operculum and an air bladder for buoyancy. Amphibia have moist skin without scales and a common chamber called the cloaca for alimentary, urinary, and reproductive tracts. Reptilia are characterised by dry, cornified skin bearing epidermal scales or scutes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each set of features with its vertebrate class gives Placoid scales and persistent notochord with Chondrichthyes, Operculum and air bladder with Osteichthyes, Moist scaleless skin and cloaca with Amphibia, and Dry cornified skin and epidermal scutes with Reptilia (A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_ANIMALKINGDOM_MATCH_Q09 - Tetrapod examples and their taxonomic classifications

questiontext.text:
Match the tetrapod genera with their correct description and select the appropriate option.

List I (Genus)List II (Description)
A. OrnithorhynchusI. Bird (Penguin)
B. AptenodytesII. Reptile (Turtle)
C. IchthyophisIII. Oviparous mammal (Platypus)
D. CheloneIV. Limbless amphibian

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Superclass Tetrapoda encompasses Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, and Mammalia, including several genera with notable evolutionary or morphological exceptions.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
Ornithorhynchus (platypus) is an oviparous exception within Class Mammalia. Aptenodytes (penguin) is a flightless aquatic bird belonging to Class Aves. Ichthyophis is a limbless amphibian belonging to Class Amphibia. Chelone (turtle) belongs to Class Reptilia.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each genus to its description gives Ornithorhynchus as an oviparous mammal (Platypus), Aptenodytes as a bird (Penguin), Ichthyophis as a limbless amphibian, and Chelone as a reptile (Turtle) (A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II).
